doc.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Dizzy Gillespie's band and sitting in with Basie in Philadelphia
summary: Dizzy breaks up his big band; Grey sits in with Basie when a trombonist is ill, fetches his horn, and is offered the England tour.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Yeah. I would dare so very strongly about that. Why because coming up with Dizzy doing things for the State Department and everything like that, we could begin to see these things. But coming on up into Basie, in which you know I spent almost 20 years of my life off and on with Basie, that’s a pretty long stint there, okay? And how I came into Count Basie’s band was that Dizzy Gillespie was going to break up his band because transportation became very big and now it was changing over to flying. And so Dizzy was bringing his big band back down to small combinations, see? But we had such a tremendous band that every one of those guys who came out of there are stars today, the ones that are left and all like that, and that was like Lee Morgan, Wynton Kelly, and Phil Woods and Melba Liston and Billy Mitchell, who I brought into Count Basie’s band see because Lockjaw left. And I got this job by going by Pep’s Show Bar in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where Basie came in to play, and I went by to see Basie’s band, and would you believe, one of his trombone players was sick that night. And this is in the days when Count Basie only used three trombones, and here there’s only two trombones. And Count Basie didn’t even know my name, but the musicians knew me. And they started pointing out into the audience, “There’s Al Grey down there in the audience down there,” and they said, “maybe he can sit in.” And this is South Philadelphia, I lived in North Philadelphia,
man I broke out of there and went to North Philadelphia and came back and I played so much that night that Basie said, “what are you doing?” “Nothing.”
So you ran and got your horn.

Yeah. I went to the north side. We lived up on North Philadelphia near the ballpark up there near the stadium on North 27th Street. I got my horn and came back and, coming from Dizzy, you know I was playing pretty strong by then, you know? So yeah, I sitted in and played music and played solos that was really outasight. And so Count Basie called me back to his dressing room and said, “well we’re getting ready to go to England in the next five days, and we’d like to take you along with us, could you make it?” I says, “I don’t have a passport, but I’ll fix a way to get one.” And so that very next morning I went all the way to Washington, DC, and got myself a passport, came back and went to New York and played my first recording with Count Basie, where it was a change in Count Basie’s band. And this is when Snooky Young came back to the band and Lockjaw Davis and I. And this is when we really changed that band all around. See because before that Basie had his band, you know and everything, but here we are now where Joe Williams was getting ready to leave pretty soon after that—
